messages.author: ba840c21971f1ac1
messages.subject: Aerial survey question
parts:
Dear Listserve,

We conducted an aerial survey on white-tailed deer and estimated the
population using distance sampling methods. The surveys were conducted
from a fixed-wing plane flown at 200 meters. We used 8 transects, flown
east to west, varying in length from 27.5 to 32.0 km. Each transect was
repeated 6 times due to the small sample size we were observing per
flight. Distances were estimated in bins 0-50 meters, 50-100, etc. with
the last distance as 250+ which is placed in a 250-300 meter bin. We
followed the directions in the User Guide (Ch 8, pg. 98-99) and used the
midpoint (e.g. 25 meters for the 0-50 m bin) as the distance for each
observation. In the analysis stage we turned the data into intervals
using the Intervals tab of the Data Filter. We pooled all the data from
each transect into one effort. The total effort was 1431 km, 150
observations and 226 deer. The density estimate came to 1.20 deer/mi2,
which is very low, even for this area. The histogram showed less than
expected on the first bin, indicating either that deer were missed or
that deer flushed and moved off the transect. I tried to attach a
picture of the histogram, but the email was rejected. However, the
detection probability was about 0.41 in the first bin, followed by 1.38
next bin and then decreasing. What do you recommend to do at this point
from an analysis standpoint? The most likely explanation is that deer
are missed on the line. However, the doesn't explain the peak in the
50-100 meter bin - if deer were missed due to habitat obstruction, then
wouldn't they be missed equally on the next bin? If deer were missed due
to the obstruction by the plane, should we subtract that distance from
all the distances and effectively move the line away from the center
line? Any advice you can give would be greatly appreciated. Thank you.

messages.author: 5140016d70f6ba82
messages.subject: Re: Aerial survey question
parts:
Elina-

You may want to refer to pgs 284-287 of the Intro to Distance Sampling.
Also, you need to provide some more details. From what you described it
isn't possible to tell whether the observers could see directly below
the aircraft. Did the plane have bubble windows or flat windows? Or
was there a belly window for downward visibility? Or was the line
offset such that 0 is really something like 72 m from the line? If the
plane has flat windows, it is my experience that the observer can only
see down to a 70 degree angle from the horizon at best. At a 200 m
flight altitude that is 72 m from the line. Also, from my experience
observers prefer not to look straight down as it is not comfortable on
the neck and it can make some people airsick. So the tendency is to
look at more like a 50-60 degree angle down from the horizon. Because
there focus is further away from the line they tend to miss the animals
closer to the line. I think that is a more likely explanation for the
histogram. You may also want to consider some of the subjects described
in the following article. I'll send a pdf separately to you.

LAAKE, J., R. J. GUENZEL, J. L. BENGTSON, P. BOVENG, M. CAMERON and M.
B. HANSON. 2008. Coping with variation in aerial survey protocol for
line-transect sampling. Wildlife Research 35: 289-298.

regards --jeff
